title: Electrum: Malicious server can replace a just-broadcast tx and try to trick user into RBF-ing it
description:
Summary

The main Electrum server the client connects to is trusted with mempool ("unconfirmed") transactions. This is documented design (https://electrum.readthedocs.io/en/latest/faq.html#does-electrum-trust-servers). [0]

However now someone figured out a way to practically exploit it:
- when the client broadcasts a new tx1, a malicious server can swallow it,
- and update the client's history with a conflicting (invalid) tx2 that replaces the outputs with the attacker's output address.
- Tx2 has invalid signatures, but this is not checked (due to light client design).
- The wallet will display tx2 as an unconfirmed transaction - tx1 will not be displayed.
- If the client then manually RBF fee-bumps tx2, the client will sign it with a higher fee, and hence pay the attacker.

Fixes

Commit 90fe30822 contains the fix [1], included in version 4.8.3.
The client now verifies the signatures of wallet.is_mine inputs for mempool txs (before adding them to its local history).

description:
Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server decompresses uploaded pipeline archives without adequately bounding expanded data in affected versions. A small ZIP or gzip-compressed tar archive can consume disproportionately large amounts of memory while the server locates or reads the pipeline file, potentially exhausting API-server resources and interrupting service.

External authentication and network controls can restrict reachability. URL-import handlers authorize before fetching and decompressing a remote archive.

The amount of expansion needed to exhaust memory depends on deployment resource limits and concurrent activity; no particular archive is guaranteed to crash every deployment.

title: Kubeflow Pipelines: Run-log endpoint permits unauthorized access to pod logs

Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server's GET /apis/v1alpha1/runs/{run_id}/nodes/{node_id}/log handler retrieves logs without authorizing the caller against the selected run. A caller who can reach the backend and knows a victim run ID and a suitable pod or node identifier can read live or archived logs using the API server's permissions.

title: @hapi/content: quadratic-time parsing of Content-Disposition parameters allows denial of service
description:
Summary

Content.disposition() takes quadratic time when a Content-Disposition parameter contains a long token without =. One unauthenticated multipart request can block the Node.js event loop for several minutes.

Details

Content.disposition() reads the parameters with a global regular expression in String.prototype.replace():

/([^\=\*\s]+)(\*)?\s*\=\s*(?:([^;'"\s]+\'[\w-]*\'[^;\s]+)|(?:\"([^"]*)\")|([^;\s]*))/g

The global scan then starts again at the next character and reads the remaining run again. The total time is proportional to the square of the run length.

title: Tornado: Quadratic CPU usage when parsing HTTP headers with line folding
description:
Summary

Tornado's HTTP header parser takes quadratic time (O(n²)) when a header value is continued across many "obsolete line folding" (obs-fold) lines. An unauthenticated attacker can send a request whose header block is mostly short continuation lines. Parsing it uses a large amount of CPU on the IOLoop thread and blocks every other connection that process is serving.

This issue is closely related to CVE-2025-67725 (GHSA-c98p-7wgm-6p64). The fix for that advisory covered repeated headers but not line-folded continuations.

Impact

All Tornado HTTP servers are affected. Header parsing runs before any application code, so no authentication or particular handler is required.

How bad it gets depends on max_header_size:

- Default (64 KB): each malicious request blocks the event loop for tens of milliseconds. Repeated requests can degrade service.
- Raised max_header_size: the cost grows with the square of the header size. A single 1 MB request can block the process for several seconds

Summary

When the ID token comes back, validate_claims only checks that the nonce exists in that table and is not expired. It does not check that the nonce was issued to the browser that is finishing the login.

So the nonce does not do its job. They start their own login to get a valid state for their session, then hit the callback with the victim's code and their own state. state passes because it belongs to the attacker's session, and the nonce in the victim's ID token passes because it is in the global table. description:
Summary

ONNX ConvTranspose shape inference performed an out-of-bounds read when the weight tensor had fewer than three dimensions and the model did not provide a kernel_shape attribute.

title: Neko: Authorization bypass in legacy WebRTC input handling
description:

title: AdminNeo: version-cache array injection causes persistent denial of service
description:
Summary
AdminNeo v5.4.1 gets the latest version from GitHub API in a browser JavaScript function. Version number is then sent by POST request to ?script=version. This endpoint lacks origin validation and accepts POST data from any source. An attacker can POST version[] parameter which PHP converts to an array. On next page load, function rawurlencode() receives this array instead of string and throws TypeError, returning HTTP 500 to all users for the next 24 hours.

Originally reported by @JoyGhoshs in Adminer: https://github.com/vrana/adminer/security/advisories/GHSA-q4f2-39gr-45jh
Although the version checking process was modified in AdminNeo, the root cause persisted.

Workaround
If you can't upgrade, make the file adminneo.version in temp directory (usually the value of upload_tmp_dir (https://www.php.net/ini.core#ini.upload-tmp-dir)) unwritable by web server.

Details
1. Intended design of ?script=version
The endpoint is designed to receive version data from GitHub via browser Jav

title: @nx/maven and @nx/gradle have OS command injection via nx.json plugin options
description:
Summary

@nx/maven and @nx/gradle spawn their project-graph analyzers through a shell and interpolate plugin options read from nx.json straight into the command line. Because a shell parses the whole line, an option value containing shell syntax is executed as a command by any nx command that constructs the project graph. Anyone who clones a hostile repository, or who checks out a pull request that edits nx.json, runs the injected command with their own privileges.

Severity

A victim who runs an ordinary nx command in an attacker-supplied Maven or Gradle workspace gets code execution as themselves. In most such workspaces an attacker who can write nx.json can already run code through the repository's build files (./mvnw, pom.xml, and the Gradle equivalents), so the genuinely new exposure is narrow — for example CI building a fork's pull request where nx.json is writable but the build files are not. We have no evidence of exploitation in the wild.

description:
Summary

An uncontrolled-resource-consumption vulnerability (CWE-400) in the Twisted HTTP/2 server lets any unauthenticated remote client exhaust server CPU over a single connection. title: charmbracelet/soft-serve: Race in SetPrivate leaves a private repository readable by unauthenticated users
description:
Summary

Soft Serve cached repository records in memory with no expiry, and trusted the cached record for every access check. SetPrivate cleared the cached record before it saved the new visibility, and not afterwards.

A request that arrived between the two read the old, public record from the database and cached it after the change was saved. From then on every access check used that stale record, so a repository the operator had just made private stayed readable by unauthenticated users over HTTP, SSH, and git:// until the server restarted.

Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can keep reading a repository after it is made private, including everything pushed to it afterwards. The attacker needs no account and no timing knowledge: a client polling GET /<repo>.git/info/refs?service=git-upload-pack, which the default anon-access: read-only allows, will eventually land in the window when the operator changes the visibility.

title: charmbracelet/soft-serve HTTP responses disclose the existence and names of private repositories
description:
Summary

Soft Serve answers Go's ?go-get=1 requests by walking up the requested path until it finds a repository, then rendering that repository's name and clone URL into a go-import meta tag. The walk checked that each candidate repository existed, but never that the caller could read it.

A request for a path inside a private repository, such as GET /secret/anything?go-get=1, therefore returned 200 naming secret and its clone URL, even though GET /secret?go-get=1 correctly returned 404. title: Waline login accepts a non-string email as a match-all MongoDB query
description:
Summary

The login endpoint POST /api/token reads the email field from the request body without checking its type and passes it straight into the MongoDB storage query. When email is not a string (for example a JSON object such as {"$ne": null}), the MongoDB storage adapter's parseWhere silently DROPS the field rather than rejecting the request, producing an empty filter that matches ALL users. The endpoint then verifies the submitted password against the FIRST user returned (user[0]), which in Waline is the first-registered user — the site administrator.

This is a PARTIAL authentication bypass, not a full one. The attacker still needs a valid password for that first user; this is not a zero-knowledge bypass and it does not disclose passwords. title: Highcharts Dashboards / Grid Pro: DataTable.setCell and column writers treat __proto__ as an existing column.
description:
Impact
When a single cell value is written to a data table, the column id is used as a key on the table's column collection without filtering, so a column id of __proto__ resolves to Object.prototype, is taken for an existing column, and the write lands at the row index on Object.prototype; a column id of constructor writes onto the Object constructor in the same way. In Dashboards releases that still supported column aliases, the id is first resolved through the alias map, so a literal __proto__ id is redirected harmlessly there, while an alias whose target is __proto__, which the connector's data table options accept, reaches the same write. An attacker who controls the column id can thereby set integer-keyed properties on Object.prototype, one per row index, holding the written value; named properties cannot be reached through these paths, because the row index is a number. title: Highcharts Dashboards: __proto__ data table id writes sync listeners to Object.prototype
description:
Impact
The data cursor keeps its listener and state bookkeeping in plain objects keyed by data table id, so a table id of __proto__ supplied in the dataPool connector configuration resolves to Object.prototype when a sync registers its listeners, and the registration creates a property on Object.prototype named after the sync state and holding the internal listener array. The property name begins with a state prefix fixed by the library, to which the sync group option can append an attacker-chosen suffix, and its value is the library's own listener array, but the property is enumerable and visible on every object in the page, and emitting a lasting state for that table id then throws, so syncs that keep lasting states, such as extremes, stop working. Exploitation requires that untrusted data reach the Dashboards configuration and that a sync such as highlight or extremes be enabled on a component using that table, which the same configuration can do.
